name: Policy profession vocabulary
description: The 100 terms for people who make and advise on government policy: evidence, appraisal, legislation, Parliament, devolution and regulation.

groups.min: term for working with ministers and the centre

cards.subject: ROAMEF cycle
says: is a model of policy-making from rationale and objectives through appraisal, monitoring, evaluation and feedback
stands for rationale, objectives, appraisal, monitoring, evaluation and feedback
cards.use: need a structured way to describe how a policy is developed and then learned from
not: is a model for how a bill moves through Parliament

cards.subject: theory of change
says: sets out how and why a policy's activities are expected to lead to its intended outcomes
makes the assumptions behind a policy explicit
cards.use: need to show why you expect a policy to work
not: is a plan for changing a department's structure

cards.subject: logic model
says: lays out a policy's inputs, activities, outputs and outcomes in order
gives a simple picture for planning and evaluation
cards.use: need a one-page picture of what goes in and what a policy should produce
not: is a statistical model that predicts spending

cards.subject: counterfactual
says: is what would have happened without the policy
is what a policy's effect is measured against
cards.use: need to judge what difference a policy really made
not: is a forecast of next year's spending

cards.subject: baseline
says: is the starting position against which change is measured
is set before a policy begins
cards.use: need to know where things stood before a policy started
not: is the final result of a policy

cards.subject: problem definition
says: states clearly what the issue is, who it affects and why government should act
comes before options are considered
cards.use: need to be clear what problem a policy is meant to solve
not: lists the preferred solution

cards.subject: rapid evidence assessment
says: is a quick, structured review of existing research on a question
trades the depth of a full review for speed
cards.use: need a fast, structured summary of what research says
not: is a full review that takes years to complete

cards.subject: systematic review
says: searches for and appraises all the relevant research on a question using a set method
aims to reduce bias in how the evidence is gathered
cards.use: need the most thorough and unbiased summary of the evidence
not: is a quick skim of a few articles

cards.subject: policy options paper
says: sets out the choices for dealing with a problem, with their costs, benefits and risks
lets decision-makers compare them
cards.use: need to put the choices to a minister or senior leader
not: states only the one option that officials prefer

cards.subject: success measure
says: states how it will be judged whether a policy has worked
is agreed before the policy starts
cards.use: need to say in advance how you will know a policy has worked
not: is a list of the people who support the policy

cards.subject: cost-benefit analysis
says: weighs the monetised costs and benefits of an option
expresses them in the same terms so options can be compared
cards.use: need to compare the full costs and benefits of options in money terms
not: counts only the cost of the cheapest option

cards.subject: net present value
says: adds up future costs and benefits after reducing them to today's value
shows whether an option gives more value than it costs
cards.use: need to compare options whose costs and benefits fall in different years
not: is the total cash spent in the first year

cards.subject: discount rate
says: is the percentage used to reduce future costs and benefits to their value today
reflects that value now is preferred to value later
cards.use: need to bring future costs and benefits to a present value
not: is a reduction in price offered to a customer

cards.subject: benefit-cost ratio
says: divides the value of an option's benefits by its costs
shows the return for each unit of cost
cards.use: want a single measure of the return for each pound spent
not: subtracts the costs from the benefits to give a total

cards.subject: sensitivity analysis
says: tests how results change when key assumptions change
shows which assumptions matter most
cards.use: need to know whether the conclusion holds if an assumption is wrong
not: checks a document for sensitive information

cards.subject: optimism bias
says: is the tendency to underestimate costs and time and to overstate benefits
is corrected by adding an allowance to estimates
cards.use: see project estimates that are consistently too hopeful
not: is a tendency to expect the worst

cards.subject: deadweight
says: is the outcome that would have happened anyway without the policy
is taken away when counting a policy's real impact
cards.use: need to remove the change that would have occurred in any case
not: is the weight of equipment bought for a project

cards.subject: displacement
says: is when a policy's gain in one place or group comes at the expense of another
reduces the net benefit of a policy
cards.use: find that a scheme's jobs were simply moved from a neighbouring area
not: is the removal of a minister from a department

cards.subject: additionality
says: is the extra impact a policy has beyond what would have happened without it
is what is left after deadweight and displacement
cards.use: need to measure the real extra effect a policy created
not: is the total spend on a policy

cards.subject: distributional analysis
says: examines how a policy's costs and benefits fall on different groups
shows who gains and who loses
cards.use: need to see how a change affects people on different incomes
not: lists the stations on a transport network

cards.subject: call for evidence
says: invites the public and experts to send information to help government understand an issue
is often used before proposals are written
cards.use: want information from experts before you decide what to propose
not: asks people to vote on a finished proposal

cards.subject: consultation guidance
says: sets out how government should run fair and effective consultations
asks for a clear purpose and for feedback on what was done
cards.use: need to run a consultation that meets government expectations
not: is a law that forces every policy to be consulted on for a year

cards.subject: equality impact assessment
says: examines how a proposal affects people with different protected characteristics
supports the public sector equality duty
cards.use: need to show that a proposal's effect on different groups was considered
not: measures a policy's effect on the environment

cards.subject: consultation response analysis
says: is the work of reading, coding and summarising what respondents said
is published with the government's response
cards.use: have thousands of responses to a consultation to make sense of
not: is the minister's reply to a Parliamentary question

cards.subject: co-design
says: involves the people a policy affects in designing it
shares power in shaping the solution
cards.use: want the people who use a service to help design it
not: means two departments writing a policy together

cards.subject: user research
says: studies how real people use or experience a service
finds out what they need before and after changes
cards.use: need evidence of what users actually need
not: is a survey of staff opinion

cards.subject: focus group
says: is a guided discussion with a small group chosen to explore views on a topic
gives depth rather than numbers
cards.use: want to explore why people feel as they do
not: is a large survey that gives statistically reliable numbers

cards.subject: public engagement
says: is involving the public in discussing or shaping government work
goes beyond informing them
cards.use: want ordinary people to take part in discussing an issue
not: is the press office's announcement of a decision

cards.subject: citizens' assembly
says: brings together a randomly chosen group of members of the public to learn about an issue and make recommendations
is designed to reflect the population
cards.use: want a representative group of citizens to deliberate on a difficult question
not: is a meeting of local councillors

cards.subject: stakeholder engagement plan
says: sets out who to engage with, how and when over the life of a policy
helps manage relationships and expectations
cards.use: need to plan how to involve the groups affected by a policy
not: is a list of people to invite to a launch event

cards.subject: primary legislation
says: is a law passed by Parliament as an Act
sets the main rules and can give powers to make more detailed ones
cards.use: need to name a law passed by Parliament itself
not: is detailed rules made by a minister under an Act

cards.subject: secondary legislation
says: is detailed law made by a minister or body using powers given in an Act
is often made as a statutory instrument
cards.use: need to name detailed rules made under powers in an existing Act
not: is a law passed as an Act of Parliament

cards.subject: commencement order
says: brings an Act, or part of it, into force on a chosen date
is needed when an Act does not take effect automatically
cards.use: need to bring part of a new Act into force
not: calls a general election

cards.subject: Henry VIII power
says: lets a minister change primary legislation using secondary legislation
is controversial because it gives ministers power to alter Acts
cards.use: see a clause that lets a minister amend an Act by regulations
not: lets a minister make decisions without consulting anyone

cards.subject: explanatory memorandum
says: explains in plain language what a bill or statutory instrument does and why
helps Parliament and the public understand it
cards.use: need a plain-language explanation of what a draft law does
not: is a list of the amendments to a bill

cards.subject: Office of the Parliamentary Counsel
says: is the specialist team of lawyers that drafts government bills
turns policy instructions into the text of the law
cards.use: need your policy turned into the legal text of a bill
not: is the committee that debates bills in the Commons

cards.subject: bill team
says: is the group of officials, lawyers and others in a department who prepare a bill and steer it through Parliament
works with ministers and parliamentary counsel
cards.use: need a team to carry a bill through its stages
not: is the team of MPs who vote on a bill

cards.subject: sunset clause
says: is a provision that makes a law or power end on a set date unless renewed
forces a review before it continues
cards.use: want a power to lapse unless Parliament chooses to renew it
not: is a clause that brings a law into force at sunrise

cards.subject: schedule
says: is a part at the end of a bill that holds detailed provisions
is introduced by a section in the main text
cards.use: need a place for detail that would clutter the main clauses
not: is the timetable for debating a bill

cards.subject: amendment
says: is a proposed change to the wording of a bill
may be moved by a minister or another member
cards.use: want to change the wording of a bill while it is going through Parliament
not: is a new bill introduced instead of the old one

cards.subject: urgent question
says: is a request for a minister to answer in the Commons on a matter of importance at short notice
is granted by the Speaker
cards.use: find that an MP has asked a minister to come to the Commons to answer on something that has just happened
not: is a question that must be answered in writing within a year

cards.subject: written ministerial statement
says: is how a minister makes an announcement to Parliament in writing
is published instead of being spoken in the chamber
cards.use: need to tell Parliament of a decision without making a speech
not: is a minister's private note to a civil servant

cards.subject: oral statement
says: is a minister's announcement made in the chamber, followed by questions from members
lets Parliament question a decision straight away
cards.use: need a minister to announce an important decision to the Commons in person
not: is a written reply to a named day question

cards.subject: Early Day Motion
says: is a motion that MPs sign to show support for a cause, and is rarely debated
is a way to draw attention to an issue
cards.use: see MPs signing a motion to show support for an issue
not: is a motion that always leads to a debate and a vote

cards.subject: whip
says: is a member of a party who organises its members and tells them how to vote
makes sure members are present for votes
cards.use: need to know who tells the MPs of a party how to vote
not: is a civil servant who counts votes

cards.subject: backbencher
says: is an MP who does not hold a government or opposition front bench post
sits behind those who do
cards.use: need to name an MP who is not a minister or shadow minister
not: is a minister who sits at the back of the Cabinet room

cards.subject: frontbencher
says: is a minister or a senior opposition spokesperson
sits on the front benches in the Commons
cards.use: need to name an MP who is a minister or shadow minister
not: is an MP with no party role

cards.subject: Opposition Day
says: is a day in the Commons when opposition parties choose the topics for debate
lets them put questions to the government on their own terms
cards.use: see the opposition choosing the subject for a Commons debate
not: is a day when Parliament does not sit

cards.subject: Prime Minister's Questions
says: is a weekly session in the Commons in which MPs question the Prime Minister
is prepared for with briefing from departments
cards.use: need to prepare the Prime Minister for the weekly questions from MPs
not: is a written answer to a petition

cards.subject: Westminster Hall
says: is a second debating chamber in which MPs hold shorter debates
does not vote on laws
cards.use: see a debate on a specific topic held outside the main chamber
not: is where the House of Lords meets

cards.subject: write-round
says: asks other departments and Cabinet colleagues to agree a proposal in writing
is used instead of a meeting
cards.use: need ministers in other departments to agree a proposal without a meeting
not: is a letter sent to the public

cards.subject: collective responsibility
says: means ministers publicly support government decisions even if they argued against them in private
keeps the government speaking with one voice
cards.use: need to explain why ministers back a decision they privately opposed
not: means every civil servant must agree with every decision

cards.subject: Cabinet committee
says: is a group of ministers that considers a policy area before it goes to the full Cabinet
settles many issues without taking up Cabinet time
cards.use: need a smaller group of ministers to agree a policy
not: is a committee of MPs that scrutinises the government

cards.subject: Cabinet paper
says: is a document circulated to ministers to inform a Cabinet or committee decision
sets out the issue, options and recommendation
cards.use: need to put an issue before the Cabinet or one of its committees
not: is a newspaper written for ministers

cards.subject: policy clearance
says: is the agreement of the relevant people and departments that a policy line can be used
happens before something goes to a minister or is published
cards.use: need to check that other departments and teams agree before submitting advice
not: is permission to enter a government building

cards.subject: red line
says: is a point a minister or government will not give way on
limits what can be negotiated
cards.use: need to know which points a minister will not compromise on
not: is a line drawn to mark a financial error

cards.subject: Number 10
says: is the office of the Prime Minister
includes advisers who shape and check government policy
cards.use: need to name the Prime Minister's office
not: is the Treasury

cards.subject: manifesto commitment
says: is a promise a governing party made in its election manifesto
is usually treated as a priority by ministers
cards.use: need to say what the governing party promised at the election
not: is a legal duty on every department

cards.subject: spending bid
says: is a department's request for money in a spending round
sets out what it will deliver in return
cards.use: need to ask the Treasury for funding in a spending round
not: is an offer a supplier makes to win a contract

cards.subject: ministerial steer
says: is a minister's indication of the direction they want policy to take
guides the options officials develop
cards.use: need to know which direction a minister wants a policy to take
not: is a minister's car allowance

cards.subject: devolution
says: is the transfer of powers from the UK Parliament to national bodies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
leaves some matters with Westminster
cards.use: need to describe how powers are shared between Westminster and the nations
not: is the abolition of local councils

cards.subject: reserved matter
says: is a subject that stays the responsibility of the UK Parliament
is not devolved to a national legislature
cards.use: need to name a subject still decided by Westminster
not: is a subject the devolved parliament has taken over

cards.subject: devolved matter
says: is a subject that a national legislature or government decides for its own nation
varies between Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
cards.use: need to name a subject decided in Edinburgh, Cardiff or Belfast
not: is a subject only Westminster can legislate on

cards.subject: Barnett formula
says: is the way changes in UK government spending in England are used to adjust funding for the devolved administrations
produces a share of changes rather than a needs-based total
cards.use: need to explain how the devolved nations' block grants change
not: is the formula for calculating income tax

cards.subject: Sewel convention
says: is the convention that Westminster will not normally legislate on devolved matters without the consent of the devolved legislature
is recognised in statute but is not enforced by the courts
cards.use: need to know whether Westminster needs consent to legislate on a devolved matter
not: is the rule that each Act must be signed by the monarch

cards.subject: combined authority
says: is a body that groups several local councils to make decisions together on areas such as transport
often has an elected mayor
cards.use: need to name a group of councils working together on regional decisions
not: is a company owned by the Cabinet Office

cards.subject: local authority
says: is a council responsible for local services such as schools and social care
is elected by the people in its area
cards.use: need to name the body that provides services in a local area
not: is a regulator of the whole of the UK

cards.subject: devolved administration
says: is the government of Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland
answers to its own national legislature
cards.use: need to name the government that runs devolved matters in one of the nations
not: is a UK government department in London

cards.subject: concordat
says: is a non-binding agreement setting out how the UK government and a devolved administration will work together
covers things like sharing information and consultation
cards.use: need the agreement that sets out how two governments will cooperate
not: is a law that settles a dispute between two governments

cards.subject: memorandum of understanding
says: is a written agreement between organisations that records what each will do
is usually not legally binding
cards.use: need to record an agreement between two departments or bodies
not: is a contract that can be enforced in court

cards.subject: better regulation
says: is the government's approach of regulating only when needed and keeping rules proportionate
asks that the costs and benefits of a rule be considered
cards.use: need to show that a new rule is justified and proportionate
not: means adding rules to cover every risk

cards.subject: regulatory burden
says: is the cost to businesses and others of complying with rules
includes time, money and effort
cards.use: need to estimate what complying with a rule will cost businesses
not: is the number of rules in force

cards.subject: regulator
says: is a body with legal powers to set standards and enforce rules in a sector
may inspect, issue guidance and impose penalties
cards.use: need to name the body that enforces the rules in a sector
not: is a minister who writes the law

cards.subject: post-implementation review
says: examines whether a regulation achieved its aims and what it cost
is carried out some years after the rule took effect
cards.use: need to check whether a rule is working as intended after it has been in force
not: is a review done before a rule is made

cards.subject: regulatory sandbox
says: lets firms test new products under a regulator's supervision with some rules relaxed
helps regulators learn about new technology
cards.use: want a controlled space where a company can try an innovation under supervision
not: is a place where regulators are trained

cards.subject: proportionality
says: is the principle that a rule or action should go no further than needed to meet its aim
balances the aim against the burden
cards.use: need to show that a measure is no heavier than the problem requires
not: means treating every case in exactly the same way

cards.subject: risk-based regulation
says: focuses regulatory effort where the risk of harm is greatest
spends less attention on low-risk activity
cards.use: want a regulator to target its inspections where harm is most likely
not: inspects every organisation equally often

cards.subject: enforcement notice
says: is a formal order from a regulator requiring someone to put a breach right
can be followed by penalties if ignored
cards.use: see a regulator order a company to stop a breach
not: is a letter thanking a firm for compliance

cards.subject: red tape
says: is a popular name for rules and paperwork seen as excessive
is what regulatory reform aims to cut where it is unnecessary
cards.use: hear businesses complain about rules that seem excessive
not: is a ribbon used at ceremonies

cards.subject: co-regulation
says: shares the job of regulating between government and the industry itself
relies on both to set and enforce standards
cards.use: want an industry body to share responsibility for rules with government
not: means two regulators fining the same firm

cards.subject: press notice
says: is a short statement issued to the media about an announcement
gives the main facts and a quote
cards.use: need to tell journalists about a decision
not: is a legal notice served on a company

cards.subject: embargo
says: is a time before which information must not be published
lets journalists prepare while keeping the announcement under control
cards.use: need journalists to hold a story until a set time
not: is the date on which a policy ends

cards.subject: rebuttal
says: is a prepared response correcting something said in the media or by others
sets out the facts and the government's position
cards.use: need a quick reply to an inaccurate claim in the press
not: is an apology issued to the public

cards.subject: communications grid
says: is the cross-government calendar of planned announcements
helps avoid clashes and plan coverage
cards.use: need to see when other departments plan to announce things
not: is the national electricity network

cards.subject: speaking note
says: is a short set of points prepared for a minister to use at an event or meeting
highlights what to say and what to avoid
cards.use: need to prepare a minister for a short speech
not: is the minister's full formal speech

cards.subject: Q&A brief
says: is a document of likely questions with approved answers
helps a minister or spokesperson respond consistently
cards.use: need to prepare someone for hostile questions
not: is a quiz for new starters

cards.subject: media handling
says: is the way a department deals with journalists and plans how it is covered
aims to keep messages accurate and consistent
cards.use: need to plan how a sensitive announcement will be handled with the press
not: is the physical handling of printed newspapers

cards.subject: statistical release
says: is the publication of official statistics at a pre-announced time
follows rules so that nobody gets an early advantage
cards.use: need to publish new figures in line with the rules
not: is a press notice about a minister's visit

cards.subject: background note
says: gives a reader the context needed to understand a subject
is shorter and less formal than a full report
cards.use: need to give someone context on an issue quickly
not: is a formal legal notice

cards.subject: stakeholder briefing
says: tells interested groups about a decision before or as it is made public
keeps them informed and avoids surprises
cards.use: need to tell affected groups about a decision before they read it in the press
not: is a briefing given to a minister before a debate

cards.subject: official statistic
says: is a figure produced by a government body or other public organisation
is expected to meet standards of quality and honesty
cards.use: need to cite a figure published by a public body
not: is a figure made up for a press release

cards.subject: UK Statistics Authority
says: is the independent body that oversees the production of official statistics
promotes and safeguards their quality and trustworthiness
cards.use: need to name the independent body that oversees official statistics
not: is the government department that sets spending

cards.subject: Code of Practice for Statistics
says: sets standards that producers of official statistics must follow
is built on trustworthiness, quality and value
cards.use: need the standards that official statistics must meet
not: sets the rules for how ministers answer questions

cards.subject: Government Statistical Service
says: is the community of statisticians working in government
is led by the National Statistician
cards.use: need to name the profession network of government statisticians
not: is the department that publishes every minister's speeches

cards.subject: confidence interval
says: is a range that is likely to contain the true value
shows how uncertain an estimate from a sample is
cards.use: need to show how precise an estimate from a survey is
not: is the exact true value of a measurement

cards.subject: statistical significance
says: means a result is unlikely to be due to chance alone
does not by itself show that a difference is large or important
cards.use: need to say whether a difference in a sample is probably real
not: means a result is important

cards.subject: correlation
says: is a relationship in which two things tend to change together
does not show that one causes the other
cards.use: see that two measures rise and fall together
not: proves that one thing causes the other

cards.subject: causation
says: is when one thing makes another happen
needs more than two figures moving together to be shown
cards.use: need to say that a policy actually produced an effect
not: is the same as two measures rising together

cards.subject: sample bias
says: is when the people in a sample do not fairly represent the population
distorts what the results say about everyone
cards.use: find that a survey reached only people who answer online
not: is a sample that is too large

cards.subject: randomised controlled trial
says: assigns people at random to a group that gets a policy and a group that does not
is the strongest way to show that a policy caused an effect
cards.use: want the most reliable test of whether an intervention works
not: compares a group with last year's figures only

qa.q: Before options are considered, what should a policy paper state clearly?
qa.right: The problem, who it affects and why government should act
wrong: The cost of the cheapest option
qa.why: A problem definition comes before options.

qa.q: Which MP is a minister or a shadow minister?
qa.why: Frontbenchers hold ministerial or shadow posts.

qa.q: Which body provides local services such as schools and social care in an area?
qa.why: Councils provide local services.

qa.q: Which office advises and supports the Prime Minister directly?
qa.why: Number 10 is the Prime Minister's office.

qa.q: You need to tell journalists about a decision. What do you issue?
qa.why: A press notice gives the facts and a quote.

qa.q: A minister has a short speech to give. What do you prepare?
qa.why: A speaking note gives the key points.

qa.q: Businesses complain about paperwork that seems excessive. What is this often called?
qa.why: Red tape is a name for excessive rules.

qa.q: Which term describes powers passing from the UK Parliament to bodies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland?
qa.why: Devolution transfers powers to national bodies.

qa.q: Which body has legal powers to set standards and enforce rules in a sector?
qa.why: A regulator enforces rules.

qa.q: In ROAMEF, what do the letters stand for?
qa.right: Rationale, objectives, appraisal, monitoring, evaluation, feedback
wrong: Review, options, analysis, minister, election, finance
Research, opinion, audit, management, execution, fund
Rules, orders, acts, motions, enforcement, finance
qa.why: ROAMEF is a policy cycle model.

qa.q: You need to show why you expect a policy to work, with its assumptions. What do you write?
qa.why: It makes assumptions explicit.

qa.q: You want experts and the public to send you information before you write proposals. What do you issue?
qa.why: It invites information to understand an issue.

qa.q: A proposal needs to show how it affects people with different protected characteristics. What do you complete?
qa.why: It supports the public sector equality duty.

qa.q: Detailed rules are made by a minister under powers given in an Act. What are they?
qa.why: They are made using powers in primary legislation.

qa.q: A party member tells MPs how to vote and makes sure they turn up. Who is this?
qa.why: The whips organise party members.

qa.q: Ministers publicly back a decision they argued against in private. What is the principle?
qa.why: It keeps the government speaking with one voice.

qa.q: Which subject is a reserved matter?
qa.why: Defence stays with the UK Parliament.

qa.q: A new rule should go no further than needed to meet its aim. Which principle is this?
qa.why: Proportionality balances the aim against the burden.

qa.q: Two measures rise and fall together. What can you say?
qa.right: They are correlated, but that alone does not show one causes the other
qa.why: Correlation is not causation.

qa.q: You need journalists to hold a story until a set time. What do you agree?
qa.why: An embargo sets a time before which it cannot be published.

qa.q: You need to put several policy options to a minister with their costs and risks. What do you write?
qa.why: It lets decision-makers compare the choices.

qa.q: You want to understand how real people experience a service. What do you do?
qa.why: It studies how users really use a service.

qa.q: You want to explore why people feel as they do about an issue with a small group. What do you run?
qa.why: A focus group gives depth rather than numbers.

qa.q: You are comparing options whose costs and benefits fall in different years. Which measure helps?
qa.why: It reduces future values to today's.

qa.q: Project estimates are consistently too hopeful. What is the bias?
qa.why: It underestimates costs and time.

qa.q: A scheme's new jobs were simply moved from a neighbouring area. What is this?
qa.why: The gain came at the expense of another place.

qa.q: Some of a policy's results would have happened anyway. What is this called?
qa.why: Deadweight is what would have occurred without the policy.

qa.q: You want to know whether your conclusion holds if an assumption is wrong. What do you do?
qa.why: It tests how results change with assumptions.

qa.q: You need part of a new Act to come into force on a chosen date. What do you make?
qa.why: It brings an Act into force.

qa.q: An MP asks a minister to answer in the Commons on something that has just happened. What was granted?
qa.why: The Speaker grants urgent questions.

qa.q: A minister announces a decision in writing instead of speaking in the chamber. What is this?
qa.why: It is published instead of spoken.

qa.q: Ministers in other departments must agree a proposal without a meeting. What is used?
qa.why: A write-round gets agreement in writing.

qa.q: How do the devolved nations' block grants change when UK spending in England changes?
qa.right: By a share of the change under the Barnett formula
wrong: By a vote of the Commons each year
qa.why: The Barnett formula applies changes proportionately.

qa.q: A group of councils makes joint decisions on transport and has an elected mayor. What is it?
qa.why: A combined authority groups councils.

qa.q: Some years after a rule took effect, you check whether it achieved its aims. What is this?
qa.why: It examines whether a regulation worked.

qa.q: A regulator concentrates its inspections where harm is most likely. What approach is this?
qa.why: It targets effort where risk is greatest.

qa.q: A survey reaches only people who answer online. What problem does this create?
qa.why: The sample does not fairly represent everyone.

qa.q: You want the strongest test that a policy caused an effect. What do you run?
qa.why: Random assignment shows cause most reliably.

qa.q: Which independent body oversees official statistics?
qa.why: It safeguards the quality of official statistics.

qa.q: You need to measure what would have happened without a policy. What do you need?
qa.why: A counterfactual is the comparison for effect.

qa.q: After removing deadweight and displacement, what is left?
qa.why: Additionality is the real extra impact.

qa.q: A clause lets a minister amend an Act by regulations. What is it called?
qa.why: It lets secondary legislation change primary legislation.

qa.q: Does Westminster normally legislate on devolved matters without the devolved legislature's consent?
qa.right: No, by convention it does not, under the Sewel convention
qa.why: The Sewel convention covers consent.

qa.q: A randomly chosen group of the public learns about an issue and makes recommendations. What is it?
qa.why: It reflects the population and deliberates.

qa.q: A firm tests a new product under a regulator's supervision with some rules relaxed. What is this?
qa.why: A sandbox is a controlled space for innovation.

qa.q: You need to see how a change affects people on different incomes. What do you do?
qa.why: It shows who gains and who loses.

qa.q: The opposition chooses the subject for a Commons debate. What is the day called?
qa.why: Opposition parties pick the topics.

qa.q: Government and the industry share the job of setting and enforcing standards. What is this?
qa.why: It relies on both to set and enforce standards.
